---
title: "How did Austie Casey get the money to pay for a factory"
---

Shareholders

The establishment of factories in Ireland followed something of a formula and Dickens Leather was not much different from other factories around the country. The anchor investor was Reginald Dickens himself who bought half of the ordinary shares the ones that came with voting privileges. That was numbers 1-6000 of the 12000 total. In accordance with the control of manufacturing act, foreign investors – i.e. from Britain – could not own more than 50% of the shares. The next two biggest investors, with 1000 each, were Austie Casey himself and Kennedy O'Brien who had already established the tannery in Portlaw. These three were joined on the board of directors by local businessman Joe Molony who bought 500 shares, with his father's business buying another 120. We can tell from the numbers associated with them that the shares were pre-allocated for Austie Casey (11001-12000) and Kennedy O'Brien (10001-11000), but they weren't for Joe Molony (7814-8313), although his pot was buttressed by another 120 shares bought by his father, A Molony and Sons, (7694-7813).

After that the ordinary shareholders included a sundry mix of investors from around the country and a much larger number of small local investors. We see investors from Sligo (380 shares), Cork, (264, 125) Kerry, (160) Leitrim (140), Tipperary (130), Wicklow (100), and another twenty odd Dungarvan individuals who bought between 20 and 100 shares. These include 75 shares for a young Perce Casey (himself a shopkeeper), local TD Sean Goulding, and local priests Thomas O'Brien (60) and Thomas Walsh (20). These were the occupations that would recur throughout the country, although one unlikely profession was a typist who bought 20 shares.

A curiosity is that Austie Casey and Kennedy O'Brien both offloaded shares soon after the factory opened. O'Brien sold half of his allocation to Dublin based Max Davis whose occupation is listed as a Company Director, and this was before the ledger book was even created. No doubt Davis had his finger in many company pies. It is not clear exactly why this was done but it seems plausible that Davis had lent O'Brien the money to help him meet the necessary target to get on the first company board. Oddly, O'Brien also sold three ordinary shares to three of audit clerks based in Dublin.

Austie Casey's shares seem a little more straightforward as he sold 123 shares to his brother Dick before Christmas of 1935. It seems very likely that this was a return of a loan, especially as Dick would continue to buy shares, a few at a time, for the next two decades. It is also notable that, with O'Brien having split his shares with Davis, Austie Casey was now the largest shareholder after Dickens.

We are still left with the question of how Austie got the money. The family lore is that he collected money from all the people he knew in the town and pooled their resources to create his own pot. He would then have given the people back their profits but gained a huge deal of power in the factory. However, there were two types of shares. The abovementioned ordinary shares did not provide the same percentage profits as the Preferential Shares.

Preferential shares were given preference over ordinary shares when dividends were being paid. They would be given a fixed dividend (perhaps 5-6%) and they had priority in the event of liquidation, and they were redeemable after a set period. However, they did not carry voting rights. They were designed to look safe and respectable, almost like a savings product, while still counting as capital for the new company. Local communities needed a way to raise capital without giving up control. In the 1930s, this structure was extremely attractive because banks were conservative and rarely lent to new industries and government grants were limited before the 1940s. P**ortlaw had managed to get a grant from the Industrial Development Capital, but Dungarvan didn't.**

Ordinary shares were thus the preserve of rich or experienced shareholders, whereas locals jumping on this new bandwagon would have bought Preferential Shares. My sense is that Austie would have roused locals and encouraged them into buying Preferential shares and had a substantial pot of his own savings, only topped up with that loan from his big brother. Austie had been medical officer in Dungarvan for two years now, as well as a practicing family doctor for almost a decade, between Cappoquin and Dungarvan. The salary of an MOH was reported as £500 and it came with a residence, namely Mountain View. Austie would have had various other bits of medical income and, if he managed to live off these, and save the salary for two years, minus the cost of the help he had, then we would have been able to save up the £875 needed for his shares. Very few people in the town had that kind of money so there wouldn't have been huge competition to buy his allocation.

How much did each share cost?

How did Austie get the money?

The question still remains
